sections.title: Geopolitics – Key Flashpoints

subsections.text: U.S.-China relations remain in a managed but fragile détente following President Xi Jinping’s September 23–25 state visit to Washington—the first Chinese presidential visit to the U.S. in over a decade and the second leaders’ meeting of 2026 after Trump’s May trip to Beijing. The sides agreed to pursue a “constructive China–U.S. relationship of strategic stability” based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity. Concrete steps included operationalizing the Boards of Trade and Investment, a reciprocal framework for more favorable tariff treatment on roughly $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction, Chinese commitments to import at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in 2027 and 2028, establishment of a bilateral AI dialogue (next round scheduled for November) plus an AI incident communication channel, and a memorandum of understanding on military crisis communications. Trump and Xi are scheduled to meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December. Fundamental frictions persist over Taiwan, advanced semiconductor export controls, rare-earth and critical-mineral supplies, and investment screening. The U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran continues (approximately day 230+), with hostilities having resumed after a June memorandum of understanding expired. Houthi forces have intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia, including repeated strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh (reportedly attacked ~20 times in October, with one incident killing 13 and injuring hundreds), Aramco facilities, and other infrastructure, alongside strikes in Yemen such as on the presidential palace complex in Aden. The Strait of Hormuz remains hazardous for commercial shipping, with multiple vessel attacks recorded. President Trump has ruled out nuclear weapons or U.S. ground troops in Iran. Over 50,000 U.S. personnel are deployed in the region under CENTCOM. Saudi-led forces have conducted extensive strikes against Houthi targets. In Ukraine, Russia has claimed significant territorial gains since early September (including more than 1,800 sq km and nearly 100 settlements, such as Dobropillia), which Ukrainian authorities describe as an “illusion,” asserting that Ukrainian forces have liberated more territory over the same period. Russian energy and infrastructure strikes continue despite a short-lived U.S.-brokered “energy ceasefire,” while Ukraine has conducted counteroffensives in Donetsk (Operation Vivaldi) that have slowed Russian pressure on the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk fortress belt. A U.S.-Russia diesel arrangement has drawn criticism from Kyiv. Advances overall remain slow relative to earlier phases of the war.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The U.S.-China trade truce originally set to expire on November 10, 2026, has been extended by two months to January 10, 2027. Overall additional U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods remain near the ~47% level reached under the earlier Busan framework (down from higher peaks). Under the Board of Trade, both sides have identified ~$30 billion of non-sensitive goods for recommended more favorable (closer to MFN) tariff treatment—U.S. examples include certain agricultural goods, seafood, wood products, cosmetics, and medical devices; Chinese examples include toys, small appliances, and holiday decorations (soybeans were notably omitted from the lists). The extension preserves the suspension of China’s expanded rare-earth and related export controls. China has recently proposed draft export controls covering a broad range of technologies, including numerous AI-related items, large language models, and other dual-use technologies (public comment period open until mid-November). The United States continues efforts to expand domestic rare-earth mining, processing, and magnet capacity, with multiple projects underway and government support.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text: Brent crude is trading in the $105–110 range (recent settlements near $109–110), elevated by the ongoing Middle East conflict, restricted flows through the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks on Saudi energy and transport infrastructure, and tight diesel markets. Global inventories have drawn significantly in recent quarters. The U.S. Energy Information Administration’s October Short-Term Energy Outlook forecasts Brent averaging ~$105/b in Q4 2026 before declining to an average of ~$84/b in 2027 as Middle East supply adapts and inventories rebuild, while noting substantial near-term volatility risk. Goldman Sachs projects Brent near $90 by December 2026 and averaging $80 in 2027 under a base case of gradual recovery, with meaningful upside if escalation persists. Coordinated stock releases and SPR-related exchanges have provided only limited relief. Short-term risks remain skewed higher given shipping attacks and infrastructure strikes.

sections.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy & Bond Markets

subsections.text: U.S. September CPI rose 0.6% month-over-month and 3.7% year-over-year (up from 3.4% in August), with gasoline accounting for more than half the monthly increase; core CPI rose 0.3% m/m and 2.6% y/y (slightly above consensus). The Federal Reserve hiked the funds rate 25 bp in September to a 3.75–4.00% target range—its first increase in three years. Markets currently price roughly 35–50% odds of another hike at the October 27–28 meeting, with higher probability of further tightening by year-end. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5.08–5.10% (having touched higher levels around 5.3% following the CPI release before partially retracing). The ECB raised its deposit rate to 2.50% in September; its next meeting is October 29. The BoJ stands at 1.25%. Elevated energy prices linked to geopolitics are a primary driver of the recent inflation uptick and have contributed to the global bond sell-off and higher yields.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Global AI-related investment is approaching or exceeding $1 trillion in 2026, led by hyperscaler capital expenditure (combined guidance from major players in the hundreds of billions). Binding constraints are shifting from pure chip supply toward physical infrastructure: power and grid interconnection (projected multi-gigawatt shortfalls in key markets), high-bandwidth memory (largely sold out through 2026 and into 2027), advanced packaging (e.g., TSMC CoWoS capacity tight through at least mid-2027), specialty materials, optical components, and cooling/water. Rare earths, gallium, germanium, and related critical minerals remain highly concentrated in Chinese refining and processing (often 80–90%+), with export-control leverage intact under the current truce extension. China has floated additional technology export controls covering AI-related items. Concentration risks also exist in lithography (ASML), leading-edge foundry capacity (TSMC), and certain passive components and industrial gases. Power availability, not just semiconductors, is increasingly cited as the near-term ceiling on deployed compute.

The Houthis have intensified strikes on Saudi infrastructure, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh (multiple attacks causing casualties and damage), Aramco facilities, and other sites, while Saudi-led forces have responded with operations against Houthi targets and claimed gains around the Bab al-Mandeb. Affordability concerns driven by energy and tariffs dominate voter focus.

subsections.text: U.S.-China relations remain in a phase of tactical stability following the late-September Washington summit between Presidents Trump and Xi. The leaders extended the Busan economic truce by two months to 10 January 2027, advanced a framework for reduced tariffs on roughly $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction, operationalized Boards of Trade and Investment, and established a bilateral “super intelligence” dialogue with a next session targeted by November plus an incidents channel. No resolution was reached on Taiwan, advanced semiconductor export controls, rare-earth licensing, or broader technology competition. Trump is scheduled to attend the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November, with a reciprocal Xi visit for the G20 in Miami in December. Rare-earth leverage continues to constrain U.S. options; China retains dominant refining and magnet capacity, and earlier export controls (with some measures suspended until November) remain a latent pressure point. The U.S.-Iran conflict, underway since late February, continues with no comprehensive settlement. Iran maintains pressure on the Strait of Hormuz through transit rules and threats to vessels using unauthorized routes; the IRGC has warned of attacks “anywhere in the region.” Multiple U.S. carrier strike groups are present or en route. Houthi forces have exploited the broader conflict to advance in Yemen, capturing territory near the Bab al-Mandeb (including reports of Perim Island) and pressuring Saudi infrastructure and shipping. Yemeni government-aligned forces have made recent local gains, but Houthi operations continue to threaten Red Sea flows that Saudi Arabia has used as an alternative after Hormuz disruptions. Diplomatic contacts via mediators (including Qatar) remain active around proposals to reopen Hormuz in exchange for sanctions relief and a path to nuclear talks; Trump has described discussions as productive and indicated no U.S. strikes before the 3 November midterms. Gaps on sequencing, nuclear verification, and frozen assets persist. In Ukraine, Russian forces continue high-intensity operations with a winter energy-infrastructure campaign already underway, while Ukrainian units have recorded localized advances in the Donetsk sector (including areas south of Lyman and east of Sloviansk/Kramatorsk under Operation Vivaldi). Russian monthly casualties remain elevated. The United States and Russia announced a temporary easing allowing Russian diesel exports (potentially several hundred thousand tons initially), which President Zelenskyy described as a gift that would be repaid with further attacks. European partners continue military and energy-repair assistance; spillover risks (airspace incidents, shadow activity) remain a secondary concern for NATO states.

Sensitive categories—semiconductors, EVs, batteries, and rare earths—remain outside the lists. Broader Section 301 issues and export-control disputes are unresolved; rare-earth magnet and related material flows stay below pre-control volumes and subject to discretionary licensing.

subsections.title: U.S.–China
subsections.text: The late-September Trump–Xi state visit remains the operative framework. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Busan trade truce, due to expire on November 10, was extended to January 10. Both sides then published reciprocal lists of nonsensitive goods worth about $30 billion each for tariff relief, and the White House said China will import at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in 2027 and again in 2028. Leaders confirmed follow-up meetings on the sidelines of APEC in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December. Delivery of rare earths and non-soybean farm purchases is still running behind prior pledges.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the Middle East
subsections.text: The war that began on February 28 is still setting the energy risk premium. Maritime sources told Reuters that Iran attacked at least 12 tankers in and around Hormuz between September 28 and October 5, the highest weekly total since the war started. Kpler data cited by CNBC put Hormuz crude exits at about 9.5 million barrels a day in the week ended Tuesday, roughly 30% below prewar norms, even as pipeline workarounds kept broader Middle East flows closer to normal. President Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November midterms, which took some of the session’s oil spike off the highs. Houthis continued to press in Taiz, cutting the last government ground line into Taiz City, and struck Aden airport; Saudi authorities reported strikes on Najran and Jizan airports. Washington is still limiting itself to intelligence support for Saudi operations rather than direct strikes.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The ground war is a stalemate with local Ukrainian gains. A monthslong counteroffensive, Operation Vivaldi, has clawed back territory in the northern Donbas and made September Russia’s worst month for net gains inside Ukraine since June 2023, according to Black Bird Group tracking cited by the New York Times. Moscow has shifted weight onto a winter energy campaign: late-September strikes hit Kyiv-region power plants, and October 8 brought deadly strikes on buses in Kramatorsk and an apartment block in Pryluky. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the same day that the deadlock could spill beyond Ukraine’s borders if either side escalates. Ukraine continues to reject land-for-peace proposals covering territory Russia has not taken.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The truce is intact but narrow. Under the current pause, China-specific tariffs sit near 30% on Chinese goods and about 10% on U.S. goods, well below last year’s triple-digit peak. The February Supreme Court ruling struck down the emergency-tariff regime, including the China fentanyl duties; the administration responded with a temporary 10% global duty under a different statute and, in July, added 12.5% duties on goods from 60 partners over forced-labor claims. The $60 billion “30-for-30” lists cover toys, holiday goods, appliances, and car seats on the U.S. side, and U.S. farm products, medical devices, and coal on the Chinese side. Exact rates and effective dates are still subject to domestic procedures. An agricultural working group is due to meet before year-end. The open variables into January 10 are rare-earth flows, the soybean and broader farm shortfalls, and whether the APEC or G20 meetings produce anything larger than another extension.

subsections.text: August CPI rose 0.4% on the month and 3.4% year on year; core CPI rose 0.3%. Fed staff put August total PCE at 3.8% and core PCE at 3.4%. sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: The spending cycle is intact and the bottlenecks are physical. TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of about NT$1.49 trillion, roughly $48.4 billion, up 51% year on year; advanced-node capacity is described as booked through 2028, with Nvidia holding a large share of CoWoS packaging. On October 8, GlobalFoundries announced a $2 billion, five-year deal to make silicon interposers for TSMC at Malta, New York — pitched as the first U.S. source of that packaging component — with volume only from the first half of 2028. BNP Paribas maps AI infrastructure investment approaching $1 trillion a year, about half in chips and servers, 20% in power, and 15% in networking. The binding constraints are advanced logic, packaging, high-bandwidth memory, lithography tools, grid interconnections, and indium-phosphide optics. Rare earths remain China’s leverage inside the truce: U.S. officials have said deliveries are lagging. Power, not model demand, is the nearer macro constraint, and it feeds the same inflation and yield pressure visible in the Fed minutes.

subsections.title: U.S.–China
subsections.text: The late-September Washington state visit produced a thin but stabilizing package. The trade truce first set in South Korea last year was extended, pushing a possible return of triple-digit tariffs and tighter Chinese critical-minerals controls out to early 2027. The Boards of Trade and Investment were operationalized. China committed to import at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in both 2027 and 2028. On 28 September both sides published lists of non-sensitive goods recommended for more favorable tariff treatment covering about $30 billion each way (77 Chinese items; more than 1,600 U.S. products, weighted toward agriculture, seafood, wood, cosmetics, and medical devices). Rare-earth and critical-mineral shipment levels remain a workstream, not a settled outcome. Two-way goods trade was $495 billion in 2025, down 25 percent year on year.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the Middle East
subsections.text: The conflict that began in late February is in its eighth month. A June memorandum on ending the war and reopening Hormuz has expired. Vice President Vance said this week that any deal requires a “meaningful” cut in Iranian enrichment, including an explanation of 60 percent material. An IRGC adviser rejected U.S. claims that Tehran has lost control of Hormuz and said the strait stays restricted until Iranian demands are met. Commercial traffic remains severely constrained: AIS-visible transits are a small fraction of the pre-crisis baseline, even as tanker-tracking firms put recent oil flows through or around the Gulf in a partial recovery (roughly 13 million barrels a day through Hormuz in late September versus about 17 million pre-war, with additional volumes via pipelines and Red Sea ports). Houthi spillover is active. Saudi authorities reported strikes on Najran and Jizan airports (three injured); Houthi media also claimed hits on Riyadh’s King Khalid airport and the Rabigh Aramco refinery. On 7 October Houthis fired missiles and drones at Aden International Airport; one landed near the runway minutes before a Cairo arrival, with no casualties reported. Saudi-backed forces say they are pressing operations around Bab el-Mandeb after earlier Houthi gains toward Perim. Washington has so far offered intelligence rather than direct intervention against the Houthis.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: Overnight 6–7 October Russia launched one of its largest combined strikes of the year: Ukrainian figures cite on the order of 70 missiles (including Iskander, S-400, KN-23, Zircon, and Onyx) and more than 100 drones. At least 25 people were killed, including children, with the heaviest toll in Pryluky (Chernihiv), where a residential block was destroyed. Energy infrastructure, defense-industrial sites, and Odesa port facilities were targeted. Ukraine’s air force reported intercepting roughly 80 percent of jet-powered drones in the wave, above recent averages. Ukraine struck a Liberian-flagged tanker off a Russian Black Sea resort (crew rescued) and an oil facility in Moscow oblast. The Kremlin criticized a French test of an upgraded nuclear-capable system as a “dead end” confrontation strategy.

subsections.text: The operative regime is a managed truce, not a settlement. The early-2027 extension avoids an automatic snap-back of peak tariffs and export controls. The $30 billion / $30 billion lists are recommendations for discussion under the Board of Trade, not implemented cuts. Agricultural market access remains a working group rather than a purchase commitment beyond coal. Sensitive technology, investment screening, and rare earths sit outside the carve-out channel. Near-term tariff risk is lower; structural decoupling and licensing friction remain the baseline.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the Middle East
subsections.text: The U.S.–Iran conflict is in its seventh month. Hormuz flows remain impaired; workarounds (East–West Pipeline, dark ship-to-ship transfers) have restored a large share of non-Iranian Gulf exports but not pre-war volumes. Iran has warned that a new U.S. strike would bring sustained retaliation against U.S. bases and that regional allies would be treated as parties to the conflict. An IRGC commander claimed on 6 October that U.S. vessels had pulled back from the Gulf, Hormuz, and the northern Indian Ocean—an assertion not independently confirmed.

subsections.title: Houthis
subsections.text: Iran-aligned Houthis have used the Iran war to reopen the Yemen front. Earlier in September they advanced toward Perim and the Bab el-Mandeb, threatening the Red Sea route Saudi Arabia has relied on while Hormuz is constrained. As of 6–7 October, Saudi authorities said airports at Najran and Jizan were struck (three injured); Houthis claimed attacks on Riyadh airport, an Aramco site, and southern targets. Saudi-backed forces, including the Giants Brigades, say they have launched a counter-offensive and that rebels are losing ground around Bab el-Mandeb. Washington has so far emphasized partner-led action and freedom of navigation rather than direct U.S. intervention in Yemen.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The war is in day ~1,686. Kyiv says long-range strikes have disabled roughly half of Russia’s refining capacity; Putin has acknowledged a GDP cost on the order of 1%. On 5–6 October Ukraine launched what Russian media called the largest drone attack on the Moscow region in two years (650+ drones), hitting oil infrastructure. Zelenskyy warned of intelligence indicating a large impending Russian strike, said a “Vivaldi” counter-offensive had retaken about 140 km² in Donbas, and reported first combat use of the domestic FP-7 ballistic missile (~250 km range). Russia has hit Kyiv bridges across the Dnipro and energy and telecoms assets ahead of winter. Germany pledged about €1 billion in military aid plus €350 million for energy repairs. Zelenskyy says he sees no sign Moscow wants talks or an energy ceasefire.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The operative framework is the extended Busan truce through 10 January 2027: suspension of the highest reciprocal tariffs and a pause on tighter Chinese rare-earth export curbs, in exchange for Chinese mineral flows and agricultural purchase commitments. Enforcement is uneven. Bessent has said soybean volumes are being met but that the separate pledge of about $17 billion a year in other farm goods is lagging; U.S. officials have also said rare-earth deliveries are behind schedule. After the Washington summit, both sides said they would pursue tariff cuts on about $60 billion of trade ($30 billion each). U.S. recommendations cover consumer goods (toys, appliances, some sporting goods); China’s list is broader and includes selected agricultural goods and medical devices, with soybeans excluded from the cut list. Sensitive items—rare earths, advanced semiconductors, AI-related technology—remain outside the cuts and under export-control regimes. A coal purchase commitment (at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in 2027 and again in 2028) was also flagged. A February 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain emergency tariff authorities; the administration has used other statutes, including a temporary global duty and later labor-related tariffs. No new broad tariff escalation has been announced since the truce extension.

subsections.text: Spot markets on 6 October had Brent near $100/bbl (about $99.9 in late snapshots) and WTI near $89/bbl, with a Brent–WTI spread around $11. Short-term bias is elevated and two-way: a Bab el-Mandeb closure or fresh Hormuz escalation would push prices higher; durable export recovery and stock releases would pull them toward the EIA’s lower 2027 path.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Hyperscaler AI infrastructure spending is estimated at roughly $775–800 billion in 2026; broader data-center capex is cited above $1 trillion. Chips and servers still take about half of the outlay, but power—not GPUs—is now the binding constraint: interconnection queues and permitting often exceed chip lead times, and data-center electricity demand is projected to roughly double from 2022 to 2026. Concentration remains extreme: Nvidia accounts for the large majority of AI accelerators; TSMC for most advanced packaging; a handful of EDA vendors for chip-design software; China for the bulk of rare-earth refining (on the order of 90%) and a large share of tungsten, gallium, and germanium processing, plus indium phosphide used in optical transceivers. The trade truce keeps tighter rare-earth curbs suspended and case-by-case licensing in place, including continued limits on military end-users, but license delays are already reported. A lapse of the truce after 10 January 2027 would re-link AI buildout, autos, and defense supply chains to Beijing’s export policy at the same time grid power is scarce.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the Middle East
subsections.text: The war remains unresolved. Tehran says the Strait of Hormuz stays closed until seven conditions in the June Islamabad memorandum are met (including a halt to hostilities and sanctions relief). Foreign Minister Araghchi has floated a plan that could reopen the strait within seven days if accepted; Washington’s response via Qatari intermediaries has not produced a breakthrough. U.S. Central Command said the Navy destroyed 13 commercial ships in the strait over the past 12 weeks under a resumed blockade. Yemen has reopened as a second front: Houthis claim ballistic-missile strikes on a Saudi Aramco refinery and Riyadh airport, while a Saudi-backed Yemeni offensive, supported by coalition airstrikes, is contesting Houthi control around Bab el-Mandeb. Fighting there is offsetting signs that some Middle East crude loadings have recovered toward pre-war levels.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: Moscow has opened its winter 2026–27 strike campaign against energy, rail, data centers, and bridges in Kyiv. A drone damaged the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro over the weekend; Russia has threatened further intensification after Ukraine vowed to double down on strikes against Russian refineries (while saying it will not target Russian civilians). German Chancellor Friedrich Merz pledged €1 billion in military aid during a Kyiv visit. A Russian drone strike near the Palanca border crossing injured a Moldovan citizen — the first confirmed Moldovan injury from a Russian drone. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev was in Washington for talks on ending the war and possible post-war energy cooperation. U.S. mediation has not produced a ceasefire; Moscow still conditions one on territorial concessions Kyiv rejects.

subsections.text: The operative framework is a short leash, not a settlement. subsections.title: U.S.–China
subsections.text: President Xi’s late-September state visit to Washington produced a managed thaw, not a settlement. Treasury Secretary Bessent said the Busan trade truce, due to expire on 10 November, was extended to 10 January 2027. Both sides then published reciprocal lists of non-sensitive goods, roughly $30 billion each, recommended for tariff cuts. Unresolved issues remain export controls on semiconductors and rare earths, Taiwan, AI competition, and China’s ties to Iran. Additional Chinese rare-earth controls that had been suspended until 10 November are widely treated as covered by the truce extension, though Beijing has not spelled that out in a dedicated notice. Separately, China has kept tight rare-earth and magnet shipments to Japan after Prime Minister Takaichi’s comments on a Taiwan contingency, a channel that also feeds U.S. and European manufacturers.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the wider Middle East
subsections.text: The war that began in late February is in its seventh month. The Strait of Hormuz remains the main physical constraint on Gulf crude. Iran-aligned Houthis have used that opening: a September coastal offensive reached Perim and Mocha, tightening their hold on Bab el-Mandeb, and fighting with Saudi Arabia has widened. Over the weekend the Houthis claimed a ballistic-missile and drone strike on an Aramco facility in Riyadh; a fire was reported. Tankers in the Hormuz approaches were also hit. Axios reported that Trump aides held closed talks at Camp David on next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi–Houthi front. Washington has so far offered Riyadh intelligence rather than direct strikes. Europe, under U.S. pressure on fuel prices, discussed releases from diesel and crude reserves (figures cited in the market included 50 million barrels of diesel and a separate crude release via IEA members).

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The war is on roughly day 1,684. Moscow has opened its winter energy campaign: the largest combined strike on Ukrainian power since last heating season hit Kyiv and surrounding oblasts around 29–30 September, and Russian drones have struck Kyiv’s Dnipro bridges, including the North Bridge, during Chancellor Merz’s visit. Zelensky said intelligence documents show a Putin directive widening strikes on civilian infrastructure, logistics, roads, schools, and hospitals, and that Ukraine will intensify attacks on Russian refineries in response while not targeting civilians. He also said a counteroffensive codenamed Vivaldi has retaken about 140 square kilometres in Donbas and is continuing. Moscow answered with threats of further mass strikes and earlier nuclear rhetoric tied to Kaliningrad. No credible near-term ceasefire track is visible.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The operative framework is the January 10 truce extension plus the $60 billion preferential-tariff lists. USTR Jamieson Greer said the U.S. list improves access for about 30 percent of U.S. exports to China. China’s list covers agricultural goods, timber, medical devices, coal, and personal-care products; soybeans were excluded. The White House said China will import at least 10 million tonnes of U.S. coal in both 2027 and 2028, about 2 percent of China’s coal imports. LNG and oil were not part of the package. The cut is narrow. Capital Economics estimates the average U.S. tariff on China only falls from about 22 percent to about 20.5 percent, still well above the roughly 11 percent level before Trump’s return. Farm purchase pledges from Busan and the May Beijing summit (including 25 million tonnes of soybeans a year through 2028) are not on track for 2026. China’s goods surplus was a record about $1.2 trillion in 2025 and, on August run-rates, was on pace to exceed that in 2026. A July 12.5 percent tariff on goods from 60 partners, including China, over forced-labour allegations, remains in the background. The February Supreme Court ruling against the emergency-tariff regime still shapes the legal basis of the current duty stack.

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: USD/JPY is trading in the high 157s to around 158 after the Bank of Japan’s 18 September hike of 25 basis points to 1.25 percent failed to hold the yen. The September Summary of Opinions cooled bets on an October follow-up; markets have shifted toward a December hike if the every-three-months pace holds. Finance Minister Katayama and Bessent have restated cooperation on “orderly” FX markets, and top currency diplomat Mimura has told markets to take the joint message at face value. That is verbal intervention so far this week, not a confirmed new operation. The precedent is real: a coordinated MOF–Treasury operation around 30 July was estimated at about ¥14 trillion ($88 billion) over two sessions, after an April–May campaign of roughly ¥11.7 trillion. Oil-driven U.S. yields and a still-wide rate gap are the main drivers of yen weakness. Intervention can spike volatility; it does not close the energy or rates gap. Broader pattern: the Fed, ECB, and BOJ are all tightening into an energy shock, which limits how far any one central bank can support its currency without importing more inflation or slowing growth.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text: At the 4 October close, WTI was about $91.03 and Brent about $102.56, a Brent premium near $11.50. The spread reflects Gulf and Red Sea disruption priced into seaborne benchmarks more than into inland U.S. crude. Prices are off the mid-September spike (Brent settled $107.63 on 10 September after Hormuz shipping attacks) but remain elevated versus pre-war levels. OPEC+’s seven core members (Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan, Oman) agreed on Sunday to hold November required output at September levels, the second straight pause after monthly target increases from April through September. Those targets are largely notional: the seven pumped about 25 million barrels a day in August, still roughly 5 million barrels a day below pre-war February levels. The next meeting is 1 November. A capacity review needed to reset quotas has slipped; sources say real quota changes are unlikely before 2027. About 2 million barrels a day of wider cuts remain in place. Near-term drivers are two-sided. Reserve releases (Europe/IEA diesel and crude) and a small U.S. crude-stock build (EIA week of 25 September: ex-SPR stocks 427.3 million barrels, +0.9 million; refinery runs 92.5 percent) lean bearish for WTI. Houthi strikes on Saudi energy assets, Hormuz incidents, and lost Gulf export capacity lean bullish for Brent. OPEC has cut its 2026 demand-growth forecast repeatedly, most recently toward 0.38 million barrels a day. Short-term bias: headline crude stays hostage to chokepoint headlines; a sustained break lower needs either a Hormuz reopening or a larger, sustained stock release. Next EIA report is Wednesday, 7 October.

sections.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy & Bond Markets

subsections.text: The Fed under Chair Kevin Warsh raised the funds rate 25 basis points on 16 September to 3.75–4.00 percent, unanimous, the first hike in more than three years. The median dot implied at least one more move this year. Officials’ year-end PCE projection is 3.7 percent headline and 3.4 percent core; July PCE was 3.7 percent headline and 3.3 percent core. The 2 percent target is not in the projections until 2029. A soft September jobs report and comments from New York Fed President Williams (“no need for urgency”) cut the probability of an October hike from roughly 70 percent to about 20–23 percent. The next meeting is 28 October, days before U.S. midterms; December remains the cleaner window if energy does not reaccelerate. Bond yields did not follow the dovish repricing: the 10-year closed Friday, 2 October, at 5.28 percent (+11 basis points on the week), the 30-year at 5.63 percent, and the 2-year at 4.83 percent. Q3 saw one of the largest quarterly rises in the 10-year in four years. The curve is pricing sticky term premium from oil, deficits, and supply, not only the next fed-funds step. The ECB raised all three key rates 25 basis points on 10 September. The deposit facility is 2.50 percent, the refinancing rate 2.65 percent, effective 16 September. Staff see euro-area inflation at 3.0 percent in 2026, 2.5 percent in 2027, and 2.1 percent in 2028. August HICP was 3.3 percent, with energy at 14.3 percent. Growth projections are 0.9 percent for 2026. Risks are higher inflation and weaker growth if the energy shock persists. No pre-committed path.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text:
AI infrastructure demand is still outrunning several physical bottlenecks at once. - Packaging. Advanced packaging, especially TSMC CoWoS, remains the tightest semiconductor constraint. Industry estimates put the 2026 CoWoS supply-demand gap near 20 percent, narrowing toward 10 percent in 2027 if in-house capacity approaches roughly 185,000 wafers a month. TSMC is adding packaging fabs, including a Chiayi Science Park expansion, and has lifted 2-nanometer wafer targets on orders from Apple, Nvidia, and other anchor customers. OSAT revenue is rising with the same cycle.
- Memory and power semis. HBM base-logic outsourcing (Micron to TSMC for HBM4E) and higher-voltage server power devices are extending lead times and supporting price increases. Optical interconnects are a parallel constraint.
- Power and labor. Grid interconnection is a multi-year gate (often four-plus years); transformers and switchgear are scarce. Behind-the-meter generation shifts the bottleneck to equipment and permits. Electrical and cooling trades are short. Bain’s 2026 work frames hyperscaler data-center capex as potentially approaching $1 trillion by 2028 if projects are not frozen by power.
- Materials. China still dominates separated rare earths and magnets. The U.S. truce extension reduces the near-term risk of the extra October 2025 controls taking effect on 10 November, but licensing of the existing seven-element regime continues, and the Japan-specific squeeze is outside that deal. Any lapse of the truce in January would hit autos, defense, and AI hardware together.
- Geography. Leading-edge logic and advanced packaging remain concentrated in Taiwan, which sits inside the same U.S.–China file as tariffs and rare earths.

subsections.title: U.S.–China
subsections.text: President Xi’s 23–25 September state visit to Washington produced an incremental package, not a reset. The trade truce was extended through 10 January 2027, pushing back a return to triple-digit tariffs and the reactivation of additional Chinese rare-earth controls. The two sides operationalized the Boards of Trade and Investment agreed in Beijing in May, recommended more favorable tariff treatment on about $30 billion of non-sensitive goods each way, and launched an agricultural working group. China also committed to import at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in both 2027 and 2028. An AI dialogue was formalized. Section 301 and 232 duties remain in place; effective U.S. tariffs on China were still estimated in the mid-20s to mid-30s percent range as of mid-year. Technology, rare earths, and Taiwan were left unresolved.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the Middle East
subsections.text: The June Islamabad memorandum of understanding expired without an extension. Iran continues to assert a permit-and-toll regime over the Strait of Hormuz; the strait remains unsafe for normal commercial traffic, with attacks continuing into early October (reports of vessels struck since late September). A U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has been in force since mid-July. Hormuz crude flows have partially recovered—tracking firms put September averages roughly in the 7–10 mb/d range through the strait, plus bypass volumes—but remain well below the pre-war baseline near 15–17 mb/d. The U.S. is reported to be sending a third carrier and roughly 9,000–10,000 additional troops, with arrival expected by late November. Over the weekend of 3 October, the U.S. struck Houthi targets in Yemen after renewed Red Sea attacks; an Iranian commander warned of a “decisive” response while denying direct direction of the Houthis. Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have begun air operations in Taiz, and Riyadh is reported to be preparing a limited coastal counter-offensive after Houthi gains around Mocha and the Bab al-Mandeb in mid-September. Those gains matter because Saudi exports have shifted toward the Red Sea while Hormuz remains impaired.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: Russia’s long-range campaign intensified into early October, including repeated strikes on the Northern and Southern bridges over the Dnipro in Kyiv, aimed at splitting the capital’s logistics. Five Russian drones, including Banderol loitering munitions, crashed in Moldova on 3 October. President Zelensky said Ukraine is testing high-speed interceptor drones and hopes to reach about 400 units by month-end, and that Putin had instructed commanders to drop restraints on the battlefield. Ukrainian long-range strikes continue against Russian launch sites, refineries, and energy infrastructure. No diplomatic breakthrough is in view.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The operative framework is the January 2027 truce extension, not a broad tariff rollback. Lists published around 28 September cover roughly $60 billion of two-way trade recommended for more favorable treatment (about $30 billion each side): U.S. agricultural goods, seafood, wood, cosmetics, and medical devices; Chinese consumer goods such as small appliances, toys, and car seats. China’s commerce ministry has said the sides aim for a reciprocal reduction framework and that most covered products could move toward MFN rates, but legal procedures and a coordinated effective date are still pending. Pre-existing Section 301/232 duties are not removed. July’s 12.5% tariffs on goods from about 60 partners over forced-labor claims remain a separate track. Rare-earth controls announced in October 2025 stay suspended under the extended arrangements through at least 10 January 2027, though August trade data still showed very thin U.S.-bound shipments of controlled compounds and magnets. U.S.–China goods trade remains well below 2024 levels.

subsections.text: The spending cycle is moving from GPU scarcity alone into a broader infrastructure bottleneck: high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, optics, power, and cooling. Micron’s CEO said this week the firm cannot meet customer demand, that supply will be tighter in 2027–28 than in 2026, and that some contracts run into 2031; first-half fiscal 2027 capex was guided near $25 billion, mostly construction. Industry commentary still frames multi-year AI capex in the multi-trillion-dollar range. DRAM pricing has surged as Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron prioritize HBM. Power is a binding constraint—Amazon’s nuclear arrangement with Constellation is one marker—alongside packaging and optical-transceiver lead times. Rare earths remain the strategic overlay: China still dominates separation and magnet production; the additional controls are suspended through the January 2027 truce, but spot export volumes to the U.S. and Japan stayed tight through August. Allied magnet capacity (including planned U.S. plants) is a late-decade story, not a 2026 bridge. Concentration risk is therefore dual: East Asian memory and packaging, and Chinese midstream rare earths.

Industry commentary still frames multi-year AI capex in the multi-trillion-dollar range. DRAM pricing has surged as Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron prioritize HBM. Power is a binding constraint—Amazon’s nuclear arrangement with Constellation is one marker—alongside packaging and optical-transceiver lead times. Rare earths remain the strategic overlay: China still dominates separation and magnet production; the additional controls are suspended through the January 2027 truce, but spot export volumes to the U.S. and Japan stayed tight through August. Allied magnet capacity (including planned U.S. plants) is a late-decade story, not a 2026 bridge. Concentration risk is therefore dual: East Asian memory and packaging, and Chinese midstream rare earths.

subsections.text: Energy, rates, and the yen are the same shock seen from three angles. Hormuz and Red Sea risk keep Brent near $100, which feeds U.S. and Japanese inflation, which keeps the Fed and BoJ tightening, which supports the dollar and leaves USD/JPY heavy enough that Tokyo and Washington remain on intervention watch. The China truce caps the left-tail rare-earth cutoff through early January and slightly eases non-sensitive tariffs, but it does not loosen the chip, packaging, or power constraints under the AI build-out—and a truce break would hit both magnets and tech simultaneously. U.S. midterm timing is relevant: reporting links further Iran strikes to the post-election window, while a third carrier is already en route.

subsections.title: U.S.–China
subsections.text: President Xi’s 23–25 September state visit to Washington produced a managed pause, not a reset. The Busan truce was extended to 10 January 2027, pushing the next hard deadline past the U.S. midterms. The new Board of Trade recommended more favorable tariff treatment on roughly $30 billion of goods in each direction (U.S. agriculture, coal, medical devices and forest products; Chinese consumer goods), with China indicating about 90% of covered items could move toward MFN rates once domestic procedures are finished. Those cuts are not yet in force. Beijing also committed to buy at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal a year in 2027 and 2028. An AI dialogue was formalized. Farm-purchase targets from the May summit remain behind schedule, and Section 301/232 duties, technology controls and rare-earth licensing stay in place.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the wider Middle East
subsections.text: The eight-month conflict remains unresolved after the 17 June memorandum of understanding expired. The U.S. is sending a third carrier strike group plus an amphibious force with roughly 9,000 sailors and Marines; the buildup is expected to be in place by late October or November. President Trump has signaled that renewed strikes are possible after the midterms. A tanker was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on 1 October, and an Iranian parliamentary committee advanced a bill that would require transit authorization and fees in the strait. Diplomacy is stalled.

subsections.title: Houthis
subsections.text: Iran-backed forces have used the wider war to press a Red Sea coastal offensive and to strike Saudi targets. The Saudi-led coalition reported a drone hit on a Medina power station feeding the Prophet’s Mosque (one transformer disabled), interceptions of ballistic missiles and drones aimed at Khamis Mushait and Jazan, and airstrikes in Taiz. Washington has so far stayed largely clear of the Yemen fight.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The war is in a winter-energy phase. Russia has resumed large combined strikes on the grid and is using jet-powered attack drones; three Kyiv bridges over the Dnipro were partly closed after repeated hits. President Zelensky said Ukraine is testing five interceptor types and aims for about 400 units by end-October, and that Putin told commanders last month there were “no rules.” Kyiv faces an estimated $27 billion defense-funding gap this year. Russia continues ground pressure and has ordered further army expansion; nuclear rhetoric around Kaliningrad drew a NATO rebuke in late September. No serious ceasefire track is visible.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The operative framework is the extended truce through 10 January 2027. Peak triple-digit tariffs and the sharpest rare-earth and high-tech export controls remain suspended, but the underlying Section 301 and Section 232 regimes are intact. The July 12.5% duties on goods from 60 partners, including China, over forced-labor claims, are a separate track. The $30 billion reciprocal carve-out lists are recommendations only; implementation depends on legal process and a coordinated effective date. U.S. officials are still pressing China on incomplete farm and aircraft commitments. China’s overall trade surplus has stayed very large as exporters reroute through third markets. The short extension keeps leverage on both sides and sets up another cliff in early January.

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: USD/JPY is trading in the high 157s to low 158s after touching about 158.44–158.50 this week, a third weekly gain despite the Bank of Japan’s 18 September hike of 25 bp to 1.25% (7–2). The September summary of opinions was read as a slower cadence, and markets roughly halved odds of an October follow-up, with December now the base case. Tokyo core CPI (ex-fresh food) rose 2.7% year on year, above the 2.4% consensus, which briefly supported the yen. Intervention so far is verbal and coordinated in tone. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura have called yen undervaluation a problem; Treasury Secretary Bessent has agreed to closer cooperation on orderly markets. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has also flagged undervaluation. There is no confirmed large-scale yen-buying operation this week. The constraint is fundamental: the Iran-linked oil shock and U.S. yields are widening the rate gap faster than the BoJ is closing it. A disorderly move through 159–160 is the practical line where actual intervention risk rises.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: The cycle is moving from a pure GPU phase into inference, networking, memory, optical connectivity, advanced packaging, power and cooling. Equipment capex outside mainland China is projected to nearly double versus the prior three-year period, but the binding constraints are increasingly upstream. Concentration remains extreme: Nvidia still accounts for the large majority of AI accelerators; TSMC for about 90% of advanced packaging; China for roughly 90% of rare-earth refining used in data-center motors and a dominant share of tungsten used in chip interconnects. Gallium and germanium exports to the U.S. are on a case-by-case license after the November 2025 truce suspended an outright ban, with a continued bar on military end-users. The January truce deadline is therefore also an AI-materials deadline. Power interconnection and transformer lead times, not chip wafers alone, are the practical limit on how fast announced capex becomes operating capacity. The new U.S.–China AI dialogue reduces the chance of a sudden rupture but does not diversify the physical chain.

Ukraine’s winter grid campaign is a separate energy-security problem for Europe but a smaller oil driver than Hormuz.

past_1_month.headline: ## Daily Macro & Geopolitical Report

subsections.title: U.S.–China
subsections.text: President Xi Jinping’s late-September state visit to Washington produced a list of eight “deliverables and understandings” covering trade, a November “super intelligence” dialogue and incident channel, counternarcotics, Iran, and symbolic items (including pandas for Atlanta). The Boards of Trade and Investment first outlined at the May Beijing summit were activated. Military crisis mechanisms, Taiwan, and guaranteed rare-earth volumes were left unfinished. A further Trump–Xi encounter remains possible around APEC in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the Middle East
subsections.text: The U.S.–Israel war with Iran, now in its seventh month, is in a tense pause rather than a settlement. President Trump has rejected an Iranian proposal that would halt hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days; Iranian officials later said they had received a U.S. response. Washington is moving additional naval force toward the region, with reporting that three carriers and two amphibious groups could be in place by late November, alongside new sanctions. Iran and its partners have used escalation for leverage: attacks on U.S. warships in the Gulf, strikes on Saudi targets, and Houthi gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including capture of a Red Sea island earlier in September. A Saudi-led coalition has intercepted Houthi drones and missiles aimed at southern Saudi Arabia and the Riyadh area. Hormuz crude transits have partially recovered (recent estimates near 13 million barrels a day), but the waterway and Bab el-Mandeb remain contestable. Saudi Arabia has pressed for U.S. action against the Houthis; the White House has so far declined a direct fight.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: Diplomacy is stalled. Moscow still conditions a ceasefire on territorial concessions Kyiv rejects. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev was in Washington this week on ending the war and possible post-war energy cooperation. On the ground, territorial change in 2026 has been limited relative to prior years (Zelensky has cited roughly 890 square kilometers taken by Russia and about 800 retaken by Ukraine). Russia has opened its winter 2026–27 strike campaign early, with large combined drone and missile packages against Kyiv energy infrastructure, including damage at the Trypillya thermal plant. Ukraine continues deep strikes on Russian refineries and defense industry. Kyiv is scaling interceptor drones against jet-powered loitering munitions and expects additional F-16s from Belgium by year-end.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The Busan truce of October 2025 — which paused triple-digit tariffs and delayed China’s rare-earth export controls in exchange for fentanyl-precursor enforcement and farm purchases — has been extended from a 10 November expiry to 10 January 2027. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent framed the two-month extension as time to pursue a larger package; Beijing confirmed an extension without initially locking the date. After the Xi visit, both sides published reciprocal lists of non-sensitive goods, about $30 billion each way (2024 import values), for tariff relief. The U.S. list leans toward consumer goods (toys, appliances, tableware, some recreational items). China’s list covers a wide set of U.S. agricultural goods (corn, wheat, meat, dairy, oils; soybeans notably not the centerpiece), medical devices, and other items, with many rates meant to move toward most-favored-nation levels. China also pledged at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal imports in both 2027 and 2028. Farm purchase commitments from the May summit remain behind pace. What did not move: rare earths, advanced technology, and other sensitive lines stay under export controls and case-by-case licensing, including continued restrictions on military end-users for materials such as gallium and germanium. Capital Economics estimates the average U.S. tariff on China only edges from about 22% to roughly 20.5%, still well above pre-2025 levels. Background measures remain: the Supreme Court struck the emergency-tariff regime in February 2026, after which the administration imposed a temporary 10% global duty under another statute, and in July a 12.5% tariff was applied to goods from 60 partners, including China, over forced-labor allegations. The truce is a deadline, not a settlement. ---.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text:
Crude is elevated and two-tiered. As of the 1 October close, benchmark reads clustered around WTI in the low $90s (roughly $91–93) and Brent from the mid-$90s to about $102–103 depending on contract, after the November Brent expiry settled near $103.50 and posted a September gain of about 14%. Prices have been volatile around headlines on Hormuz and diplomacy; the 52-week Brent range runs from the high $50s to about $107. Drivers:
- Partial recovery of Gulf crude flows. JPMorgan has estimated regional crude shipments near 17.5 million barrels a day, about 98% of pre-war levels, while refined-product flows were only about 58%. Hormuz transits have rebounded; Saudi East–West pipeline capacity has been partly restored.
- Product tightness. Attacks linked to the Iran and Ukraine wars have cut refining capacity. China has suspended oil-product exports beyond Hong Kong and Macau, removing flexible diesel and gasoline supply. The U.S. has been urging European allies to draw emergency diesel stocks and is near the end of a coordinated SPR release (up to 40 million barrels cited as the last tranche).
- OPEC+ held October required production at the September level (6 September decision). The next meeting is 4 October.
- U.S. commercial crude stocks were 427.3 million barrels for the week ending 25 September (up 0.9 million). Retail gasoline has been near $4.46 a gallon. Short-term outlook: crude balances can loosen if Hormuz volumes hold and waivers on Iranian loadings continue, which is why some physical benchmarks have softened into contango. Products are the tighter market into winter. Upside risks are a renewed U.S. strike campaign, Houthi disruption at Bab el-Mandeb, or another Hormuz closure. Downside risks are a credible ceasefire and a faster product-export restart from China and the Gulf. ---.

sections.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy & Bond Markets

subsections.text:
The global bond sell-off is the macro center of gravity. The U.S. 10-year yield touched 5.34% on 1 October, the highest since 2002, before easing to about 5.26–5.27%. The 2-year was last near 4.81%. The third-quarter rise in the 10-year was the largest since 1994. France’s 10-year has approached 5%; Britain’s 30-year has crossed 6%, the highest since 1998. Japan’s yields have moved up with the pack. Inflation is being re-accelerated by energy. Softer U.S. August inflation details did not calm the long end. Euro-area national prints for September beat forecasts: Germany 3.3%, France 3.4%, Italy 4.1%, with the bloc expected near 3.6% versus 3.2% in August. Core in Germany was steady at 2.4%. Policy:
- The Fed hiked last month. Futures still price a meaningful chance of another move at the 28 October meeting (on the order of one-in-three) and further hikes into 2027. Stronger growth, including AI-related capex, is cited alongside oil as a reason not to ease.
- The ECB raised all three key rates by 25 basis points on 10 September, taking the deposit rate to 2.50%. Staff projections put headline inflation at 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027, and 2.1% in 2028. Markets have priced several further hikes over the next year. The euro-area flash HICP is due today.
- The BoJ is at 1.25%, with the next hike more likely in December than October (see section 3). Higher real yields are tightening financial conditions even without another immediate hike, and they raise the fiscal cost of funding deficits in the U.S., France, the U.K., and Japan. ---.

The third-quarter rise in the 10-year was the largest since 1994. France’s 10-year has approached 5%; Britain’s 30-year has crossed 6%, the highest since 1998. Japan’s yields have moved up with the pack. Inflation is being re-accelerated by energy. Softer U.S. August inflation details did not calm the long end. Euro-area national prints for September beat forecasts: Germany 3.3%, France 3.4%, Italy 4.1%, with the bloc expected near 3.6% versus 3.2% in August. Core in Germany was steady at 2.4%. Policy:
- The Fed hiked last month. Futures still price a meaningful chance of another move at the 28 October meeting (on the order of one-in-three) and further hikes into 2027. Stronger growth, including AI-related capex, is cited alongside oil as a reason not to ease.
- The ECB raised all three key rates by 25 basis points on 10 September, taking the deposit rate to 2.50%. Staff projections put headline inflation at 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027, and 2.1% in 2028. Markets have priced several further hikes over the next year. The euro-area flash HICP is due today.
- The BoJ is at 1.25%, with the next hike more likely in December than October (see section 3). Higher real yields are tightening financial conditions even without another immediate hike, and they raise the fiscal cost of funding deficits in the U.S., France, the U.K., and Japan. ---.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text:
Hyperscaler capex remains the main private-demand shock. The IEA has noted that spending by the largest technology firms exceeded $400 billion in 2025 and is expected to rise on the order of 75% in 2026, larger than global upstream oil and gas investment. Bain’s data-center work points to multi-trillion-dollar build-out needs by 2030 if announced compute plans are met. U.S. data-center power demand is forecast to rise from about 31 GW in 2025 toward 41 GW in 2026 and 66 GW in 2027, with only about 60% of near-term scheduled capacity expected on time. Concentration risks:
- Accelerators: Nvidia still accounts for the large majority of AI accelerator chips.
- Foundry and packaging: TSMC produces about 90% of advanced packaging that integrates logic and memory.
- Lithography: ASML remains the sole EUV supplier.
- Memory: Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have shifted capacity to high-bandwidth memory. IDC has projected DRAM revenue up about 177% in 2026; contract prices for conventional DRAM have seen extreme quarter-on-quarter jumps. New capacity is years out, so tightness can run into 2027.
- Materials: China processes roughly 99% of gallium, about 90% of rare-earth metals used in magnets, and a dominant share of tungsten. The truce to 10 January improved the licensing climate versus the autumn 2025 controls, but there are no published volume guarantees, and military end-uses remain restricted. U.S. processing projects cannot replace Chinese supply on this horizon.
- Power and grid equipment: interconnection queues, transformers, and turbines are now binding constraints alongside chips. The Washington “super intelligence” dialogue is a political channel, not a supply commitment. Export controls on leading-edge tools and chips remain the structural fault line under the tariff truce. ---.

subsections.text: The same three shocks are feeding each other. The Iran war keeps oil and diesel tight, which re-accelerates inflation, which forces the Fed, ECB, and BoJ to stay tight, which pushes global yields to multi-decade highs and keeps the yen under pressure near intervention territory. The U.S.–China truce lowers the odds of a simultaneous rare-earth and tariff shock through early January, which is what allows the AI build-out to proceed, but that build-out is itself a source of power demand, copper and electrical-equipment inflation, and political sensitivity around technology controls. Ukraine’s winter energy campaign adds a second refined-product risk on top of the Gulf. A Hormuz relapse would hit yields, the yen, and AI power costs at once.

past_1_month.headline: ## Daily Macro & Geopolitical Report
past_1_month.summary: Markets open Q4 against a three-front backdrop: a seven-month U.S.–Iran war that still prices a Hormuz/Red Sea risk premium; a ceremonial but thin Trump–Xi state visit that bought two extra months of trade calm; and a synchronized hawkish turn at the Fed, ECB, and BOJ as energy and AI-related demand keep inflation above target. U.S. midterms in November now sit on top of all three.

subsections.title: U.S.–China / Trump–Xi
subsections.text: Xi Jinping’s late-September state visit to Washington was the third leader-level meeting since Trump returned to office. Ceremony exceeded substance. The two sides extended the existing trade truce to 10 January 2027, launched a modest “30-for-30” tariff-cut list on non-sensitive goods, opened an AI-safety dialogue, and booked Chinese purchases of U.S. coal. Taiwan, Iran, rare earths, and leading-edge chips were discussed without a public bargain. Xi pressed Washington to “oppose” Taiwan independence; Taipei rejected the framing. Beijing continues to trade with Tehran and has not used its Russia leverage the way Washington wants.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the wider Middle East
subsections.text: The war that began 28 February 2026 is approaching month eight. Diplomacy is live but brittle: a seven-day Iranian trust-building plan is circulating via Qatar, sequencing remains the sticking point, and Trump still says the U.S. will “win very soon” while threatening to “annihilate” the regime if talks fail. Fresh U.S. sanctions hit procurement networks in Russia, China, Hong Kong, and Pakistan. Iran’s rial printed new lows. Houthis have expanded control along Yemen’s west coast and the Bab al-Mandeb, stepped up Red Sea attacks, and struck toward Saudi’s East-West/Yanbu corridor—the main Hormuz workaround. WHO reports 800+ killed in renewed Yemen fighting over two months. U.S. forces were due to leave remaining Iraqi bases this week. China remains Tehran’s economic backstop and, per reporting, a major source of dual-use components seized en route to the Houthis.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The war is past day 1,680. Russian drone and missile waves on Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other cities continued through UNGA week; Zelenskyy called the pattern “terrorism” and said Putin keeps inventing excuses not to talk. Putin says all settlement ideas remain “on the table” but Russia will first weigh its interests after Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory and polling sites. Trump publicly told Zelenskyy to “settle with Putin.” A limited energy-infrastructure ceasefire has not stuck. Washington locked in remaining FY2026 Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative funds (~$93 million of a $400 million package) before the 30 September deadline. Putin ordered further army expansion; Zelenskyy warned of more North Korean deployments and $12 billion in planned Russian jet-drone spending. NATO has condemned Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric around Kaliningrad. Winter energy targeting is the next operational risk.

subsections.title: Other
subsections.text: UNGA highlighted institutional strain: Xi skipped New York for Washington; a search is underway for António Guterres’s successor at year-end. APEC in Shenzhen (18–19 November) is the next leader calendar date; talk of a Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral remains unscheduled.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text:
The Busan-origin truce that capped reciprocal escalation (roughly 30% on many Chinese goods / 10% on many U.S. goods, plus a rare-earths flow arrangement) is now extended from a 10 November expiry to 10 January 2027. That is a two-month bridge, not a reset. After the summit, both sides published “non-sensitive” lists totaling about $60 billion ($30 billion each) recommended for more favorable tariff treatment via a new U.S.–China Board of Trade: - U.S. list (77 Chinese items): toys, holiday décor, fishing gear, tableware, small appliances, car seats.
- China list (~1,619 U.S. items): a wide agricultural basket (soybeans still a notable omission from some cuts), medical devices, coal-related products, personal care. China also committed to import at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in 2027 and again in 2028. Financial-services access and farm purchase tracking remain under discussion; Beijing is behind earlier farm-purchase run-rates. Average U.S. tariffs on China may ease only modestly (one estimate: ~22% to ~20.5%) and stay well above pre-2025 levels. Sensitive items—advanced chips, dual-use tech, critical minerals outside the truce channel—stay outside the goodwill list. The January 10 clock is the next hard date. ---.

subsections.title: Yen
subsections.text: USD/JPY is around 157 after a July spike toward 164 (40-year lows). Japan and the U.S. Treasury staged a coordinated yen-buying operation in late July (reports in the $50–90+ billion range depending on the window). A separate April–May campaign totaled a record ~¥11.7 trillion. MOF data show no intervention between 27 August and 28 September; verbal defense has done the recent work. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and vice minister Atsushi Mimura have restated that yen undervaluation is “problematic” and that Tokyo is working with Washington. Markets treat 160 as the line that revives live intervention risk.

subsections.title: BOJ
subsections.text: On 18 September the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate 25 bp to 1.25%—a 31-year high—in a 7–2 vote. The hike was not enough, on its own, to re-anchor the yen because the Fed funds range is 3.75–4.00%. Another BOJ move is widely mapped to the 30 October meeting or December if inflation and U.S. pressure persist.

subsections.title: Broader FX
subsections.text: Rate differentials still favor the dollar versus JPY and still-negative or low-rate peers. Intervention is now explicitly a G2 coordination tool, not a solo Japanese circuit-breaker. Carry-trade positioning remains a two-way risk if 160 breaks or if the BOJ accelerates.

subsections.title: Levels (late 30 September prints; highly volatile)
subsections.text: One live Hormuz-crisis tape showed Brent ~$97–98 and WTI ~$90, with a wide seaborne-vs-inland spread. Other sessions in the last 10 days printed Brent from the mid-$90s to above $110 depending on pipeline and transit headlines. The consistent story is a war premium over a recovering-but-not-normal Gulf export base, not a pre-February 2026 $70s market.

subsections.title: Drivers
subsections.text:
- Partial Hormuz disruption plus Houthi pressure on Bab al-Mandeb and Saudi’s East-West/Yanbu system.
- Offset: Middle East seaborne exports recovering toward ~80%+ of pre-war run-rates in September as Saudi pipeline capacity comes back in stages; Iranian loadings have also recovered under waiver talk.
- U.S. SPR releases have met soft demand; Cushing stocks are tight, supporting WTI relative to Brent at times.
- China crude intake earlier in the summer ran well below year-ago levels, capping how far flat price could run even in a deficit tape.

subsections.title: Risks and short-term outlook
subsections.text: Upside: a failed Doha track, a new strike on Yanbu or East-West, tighter Houthi control of Bab al-Mandeb, or winter European diesel tightness. Downside: a durable U.S.–Iran pause, faster Hormuz transits, and Chinese demand staying soft. Base case used by several houses is elevated-but-choppy prices through Q4—high $70s to low $90s on a “normalization” path, $90–100+ if the security environment stays the operating regime. Diesel cracks and European gas remain the consumer-price transmission channel.

subsections.title: Inflation
subsections.text: U.S. CPI August: +3.4% y/y, +0.4% m/m; core CPI +2.4% y/y, +0.3% m/m. Energy +2.1% m/m; gasoline +3.9% m/m. PCE August (released 30 September): +0.3% m/m, +3.4% y/y; core PCE about +3.0% y/y—softer than some forecasts, still far from 2%. Euro area HICP has been running in the high-2s to low-3s and is expected to jump again on energy in the September flash. Japan’s inflation remains above the BOJ’s 2% target, amplified by the weak yen.

subsections.title: Policy
subsections.text:
- Fed (17 September): +25 bp to 3.75–4.00%, first hike since 2023, unanimous. Median 2026 funds rate lifted to 4.1%. Several officials still flag one more hike this year; October 28 is live but not locked after the softer PCE print.
- ECB (10 September): +25 bp, deposit facility 2.50%. Lagarde called it a “no-brainer.” Next meeting 29 October.
- BOJ (18 September): +25 bp to 1.25%. Next: 30 October.
- RBA: hiked to 4.60%.

subsections.title: Bonds
subsections.text: U.S. 10-year around 5.24–5.26% (29–30 September), up more than 100 bp year-to-date in some tallies; 30-year has traded 5.5–5.6%, multi-decade highs. German 10-year ~3.6%; UK 10-year ~5.4%; JGB 10-year ~3.1%. Mortgage rates above 7% in the U.S. Treasury buybacks in the long end have not capped the sell-off. Energy + AI capex + fiscal supply + a hiking Fed is the common explanation.
Hyperscaler and lab capex is still scaling toward hundreds of billions in 2026 and multi-trillion cumulative buildout estimates through the early 2030s. Constraints are no longer just GPUs.

subsections.title: Concentration
subsections.text:
- Accelerators: Nvidia still dominant in training silicon.
- Foundry / advanced packaging: TSMC remains the bottleneck for leading-edge logic and CoWoS-class packaging; Arizona capacity is years from substituting Taiwan at scale.
- Memory: HBM/DRAM tightness; DRAM revenue forecasts have been revised sharply higher for 2026; Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron have reallocated capacity to HBM.
- Substrates / ABF / PCBs: multi-year shortage talk into 2028–30.
- Critical minerals: China still refines the large majority of rare earths used in motors and cooling; gallium, germanium, tungsten licensing and prior export bans remain a live geopolitical switch. The trade truce only pauses some of that weaponization.
- Power and labor: grid interconnection, transformers, electrical trades, and cooling specialists now delay projects as much as chips. Data-center power demand is colliding with wartime munitions demand for the same industrial base (e.g., Patriot interceptor rebuild vs. rare-earth and packaging capacity).

subsections.title: Financial layer
subsections.text: A growing share of the build is moving from hyperscaler cash into leases, private credit, and structured vehicles. That raises cyclical and refinancing risk if model-revenue ramps disappoint or if rates stay at 5%+ on the long end. Export-control divergence (U.S. chip rules vs. Chinese mineral rules) is the strategic overlay the Trump–Xi AI dialogue has not resolved.

Oil is the hinge. A hotter Iran/Houthi tape lifts gasoline and diesel, holds CPI/PCE above target, keeps the Fed/ECB/BOJ hawkish, supports USD/JPY weakness and yen-intervention risk, and tightens financial conditions into an AI capex boom that already needs cheap power and patient capital. China sits in every channel: rare-earths and packaging for U.S. weapons and AI servers; oil demand that caps crude; diplomatic cover for Iran and Russia; and the January 10 tariff clock. A “stability bargain” (trade truce + coal/farm buys + AI talk) can coexist with proxy conflict. That is the current equilibrium. It breaks if Hormuz/Bab al-Mandeb closes harder, if rare-earth licenses are pulled, or if a Taiwan incident forces the security agenda over the commercial one.

past_1_month.headline: Daily snapshot as of early Wednesday Asia time.
past_1_month.summary: Daily snapshot as of early Wednesday Asia time. Markets are digesting last week’s Trump–Xi state visit, a still-unresolved seven-month U.S.–Iran war that is spilling into Yemen and the Red Sea, a firming U.S. rates complex, and oil that remains elevated even as some Gulf export volumes recover.

subsections.title: U.S.–China / Trump–Xi
subsections.text: The three-day Washington state visit (24–25 September) was heavy on ceremony and light on binding outcomes. Both sides framed the relationship as “strategic stability” and “no conflict, no confrontation,” but analysts describe a tactical pause rather than a reset. Concrete items: an AI-incident communication channel with a dedicated dialogue slated for November; work on military crisis communications; operationalization of the U.S.–China Boards of Trade and Investment; and two further leader meetings already booked—APEC in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December. Taiwan was raised (Xi pressed for U.S. “prudence”); there was no public resolution on arms sales. Talks also touched Iran and Ukraine. Trump has publicly rejected deeper joint AI-safety work even as the incident channel was announced.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the wider Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The U.S.–Israeli campaign against Iran, underway since late February, is in its seventh month. Hormuz remains the core oil-and-gas chokepoint; Iran has used restricted zones, mines, and the threat of further disruption as leverage. Indirect contacts via Qatar and other mediators resumed around UNGA; Washington rejected an Iranian proposal that largely restated earlier terms and did not add meaningful nuclear or strait concessions. Trump has kept three public options on the table—deal, economic strangulation, or much wider force—while denying that the U.S. has offered sanctions relief as a precondition. Yemen is the new second front. After months on the sidelines, the Houthis seized the remaining government-held Red Sea coastline, Mokha, and the Hanish islands in early–mid September, putting Iranian-aligned forces close to the Bab al-Mandab. They have since struck Saudi military and energy sites (including the Riyadh area). The U.S. says it is in direct contact with the Houthis and that the group claims it does not want a fight with Washington; Riyadh has asked for U.S. strikes and has not received them. Saudi- and Yemeni government-aligned forces are now hitting Houthi missile/drone cadres and logistics. The dual-chokepoint risk (Hormuz plus Bab al-Mandab) is the main geopolitical premium in energy.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The war of attrition continues. Russia is running large jet-powered drone and missile waves against Kyiv and other cities (the National Academy of Sciences building was hit; data centers and logistics have been targeted). Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps says Operation Vivaldi has retaken about 176 km² north of Lyman across three phases. Moscow is raising 2027 defense spending by a reported 27% and has restricted publication of refinery and energy data after Ukrainian long-range strikes. Drones near the Polish border have prompted Warsaw to revisit air-defense rules of engagement. Neither side is signaling a ceasefire.

subsections.title: Other
subsections.text: Follow-up Trump–Xi meetings in November–December are now the main scheduled pressure valves in the U.S.–China calendar. Midterm politics in the U.S. (November) constrain how much either leader will give before then.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The year-old tariff truce—U.S. rates on Chinese goods around 30%, Chinese rates on U.S. goods around 10%, plus rare-earth access and agricultural purchase pledges—has been extended two months, to 10 January 2027. That is a short bridge through U.S. midterms and the two remaining 2026 summits, not a durable deal. Under the new Board of Trade “30-for-30” framework, each side recommended about $30 billion of non-sensitive goods for more favorable tariff treatment (~$60 billion two-way). U.S. cuts cover consumer items (toys, fireworks, holiday décor, small appliances, child seats). China’s list covers a wide set of U.S. farm and related products (corn, dairy, meats, some medical devices and materials) but not soybeans. China also agreed to take at least 10 million tonnes of U.S. coal in each of 2027 and 2028. Implementation still requires domestic legal steps; there is no firm start date. What was left off matters more: advanced chips, EVs/batteries, and rare earths. Bessent has said China is meeting the 25 million-ton soybean pledge but lagging other agricultural commitments (~$17 billion). The structure is a managed pause while both sides buy time. ---.
